title: Routing Anonymity and Identifiability of Noisy Quantum Hardware
abstract: Present-day quantum computing is cloud-based, where a user submits a circuit to a service provider's proprietary backend hardware. While providers may wish to hide implementation details, scheduling choices, or even which physical device was used, noisy finite-shot outputs can carry backend-specific fingerprints: information imprinted in the classical output distribution that can reveal the backend identity. So far, such fingerprints have mostly been studied from a benchmarking perspective, with limited attention to privacy considerations for users and providers. This work develops the first formal framework for backend identifiability and its privacy implications. We introduce a backend-identifiability game and use it to formalise routing anonymity as a security notion for quantum cloud services. We show that backend identifiability is a hypothesis-testing problem and prove that, under passive i.i.d. access to a single backend, routing anonymity decays exponentially at the Chernoff rate. We also establish a utility-anonymity trade-off, imposing fundamental limits on how much backend-specific information can be removed from classical outputs without degrading their usefulness. In addition, we observe that, for noisy quantum hardware, identifying fingerprints are inherently an intermediate-depth phenomenon, and establish a depth principle using Pauli-transfer-matrix tools. We complement the theory with experiments on Amazon Braket on AWS, using ion-trap and superconducting quantum processors. We observe 87-90% classification between superconducting backends and 96-100% classification across physical platforms, and find that identifiability can survive natural forms of post-processing. Overall, these results establish routing anonymity as a distinct security requirement for quantum cloud computing, and provide a framework for quantifying and controlling the utility-anonymity trade-off.
summary: This paper formalizes backend identifiability in cloud quantum computing, proposing 'routing anonymity' as a necessary security measure. It develops theoretical bounds on how much information can be hidden while maintaining utility and validates these findings with experiments showing high device distinguishability on real hardware.
main_problem: The work develops a formal framework for backend identifiability, addressing how classical outputs from noisy quantum hardware can leak information about the service provider's specific physical device or routing choices.
main_result: It establishes 'routing anonymity' as a distinct security requirement for quantum cloud services and quantifies the fundamental utility-anonymity trade-off in this context.
method: The authors introduce an operational backend-identifiability game, formalizing the problem as hypothesis testing, and use tools like Pauli-transfer-matrices to analyze noise structure.
model_or_system: The study models cloud-based quantum computing (QaaS) where users submit circuits to proprietary backends. Experiments are conducted on real hardware platforms like Amazon Braket using ion-trap and superconducting processors.
key_observables: Backend-specific 'fingerprints' imprinted in the classical output distribution, classification accuracies of device identity, and leakage rates measured by Chernoff information.
important_parameters: The analysis considers circuit workload, finite-shot resolution, repeated access patterns, and post-processing capabilities.
main_assumptions: Theoretical results assume passive i.i.d. access for certain analyses; the framework is designed to handle provider post-processing while maintaining security notions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate classification performance across varying circuit depths (intermediate-depth principle) and demonstrate temporal leakage by showing how LSTMs can forecast noise distributions from sequential measurements.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the problem via toy examples (Lock-and-Key, Tokens) to developing a formal game theory framework for routing anonymity. It then proves theoretical bounds (Chernoff decay, utility-anonymity trade-off) and validates these concepts with extensive experiments on real quantum hardware.
why_interesting: It provides rigorous security metrics for the practical deployment of quantum computation services, moving beyond algorithmic complexity to address physical implementation vulnerabilities relevant to open quantum systems characterization.
